title: Louvois and Louis XIV to Catinat, seven Grand Chiffre despatches, 8 July - 14 Sept 1691 (Mémoires de Catinat 1819, t. II pp. 295-342)

steps.what: Fetched MDZ hOCR and IIIF page images of Mémoires de Catinat t. II.
Tokenised the figures from the hOCR, dropping specks, running heads and show-through glyphs; split into seven letters.
Applied Bazeries' 1893 Grand Chiffre table and segmented the output with a period lexicon.
Aligned the decode of L1 and L3 with Bazeries' clear text: 98.1% and 99.1% of characters.
Checked 137 doubtful stretches on page crops; 7 OCR errors and 3 dates corrected.
Read all seven letters, five of them for the first time in print.

Full texts listed in outcome.texts (George Lasry's request of 22 Oct 2026): letters/L1-L7.txt each carry the word-segmented decryption and, below it, the groups as printed (the transcription); key_file points to Bazeries' Grand Chiffre table as transcribed in ../feuquieres/grand_chiffre_1691.tsv (the context readings of blank entries are not tabulated separately).

Verification 5 (plain-bar rows): L2, L5 and L6 had been scored on the segmenter's unpunctuated runs (plain 0.50/0.579/0.562). Word division re-done by hand on the decodes (values unchanged, doubtful groups marked [?]), letters/L2_reading.md, L5_reading.md, L6_reading.md: plain 0.833/0.906/0.724, explicit 0.939/0.938/0.862. Keep read.

outcome.method_basis: Bazeries' 1893 reconstruction of the Grand Chiffre (Le Masque de fer), built from these very Catinat despatches, was applied to OCR'd figures from the 1819 Mémoires de Catinat; Bazeries' clear texts of L1 and L3 served as controls (98.1% and 99.1%).
outcome.notes: Seven groups unread (six misprinted above 587, one damaged); about a hundred blank-table groups read from context.

credits.note: Grand Chiffre table (Le Masque de fer, 1893) applied; his clear texts of L1 and L3 used as controls

texts.label: L1, Louvois to Catinat, Versailles, 8 Jul 1691
texts.summary: The King is surprised the news of Coni came by the post and not by courier; Bulonde is to be arrested and taken to the citadel of Pignerol, shut in a room at night and free by day to walk the ramparts "avec un masque"; fortify Carmagnole, destroy Quiers and Villeneuve d'Ast if they cannot be held. As Bazeries printed it (1893).

texts.label: L2, Louvois to Catinat, Versailles, 9 Jul 1691
texts.summary: After the failure at Coni: fortify Carmagnole, burn the places the enemy could hold in winter (Villeneuve d'Ast, Quiers), seek a battle before the Germans arrive and avoid one after; the King prescribes nothing but "vous ouvre seulement des vues". New beyond the first 130 groups Bazeries printed.

texts.label: L3, Louis XIV to Catinat, Versailles, 19 Aug 1691
texts.summary: Carmagnole's weakness, Caraffa's foresight in stocking grain, Chamlay sent out with the King's full intentions; pull the grain of Saluces, Savillan and Fossano into Carmagnole or Pignerol. As Bazeries printed it.

texts.label: L4, Louis XIV to Catinat, 24 Aug 1691
texts.summary: Chamlay is to weigh with Catinat every course open in the war; the Rome negotiation makes it desirable to prolong the army's stay beyond the mountains; Casale to be palisaded and supplied; the King hopes Carmagnole can be kept and Coni taken at the end of the campaign; Pignerol's safety is "le premier objet".

texts.label: L5, Louis XIV to Catinat, 29 Aug 1691
texts.summary: Proposals for a treaty with the people of Mondovì may be concluded as Catinat judges; the enemy is reported to seek passage by Geneva or the Valais into the Chablais; la Hoguette keeps his troops at Suze; do not go far from Carmagnole for supplies.

texts.label: L6, Louis XIV to Catinat, Versailles, 6 Sept 1691
texts.summary: The only road to Casale in winter is by Genoa and unsafe; Larray has sent an Irish battalion to Briançon fearing the Barbets; if Catinat is to pass the Po, do it before the enemy moves; Chamlay has arrived.

texts.label: L7, Louis XIV to Catinat, Fontainebleau, 14 Sept 1691
texts.summary: After Chamlay's report the King decides "à préférer le parti solide à l'honorable": recross the mountains at the end of the campaign, not return to Piedmont in 1692, and fight a defensive war in the Alpine cols, while prolonging the campaign and keeping Carmagnole as long as possible for the negotiation with the Pope and the Italian states; then attack Coni.
